answer:
Yes. Label rows \(1,\dots,7\) from top to bottom and columns \(1,\dots,9\) from left to right. Suppose the two opposite removed corners are \((1,1)\) and \((7,9)\). Remove the additional square \((1,8)\).

The remaining \(60\) squares can be tiled as follows:

- In row 1, place horizontal dominoes on  
  \[
  (1,2)(1,3),\quad (1,4)(1,5),\quad (1,6)(1,7),
  \]
  and one vertical domino on \((1,9)(2,9)\).
- In row 2, place horizontal dominoes on  
  \[
  (2,1)(2,2),\quad (2,3)(2,4),\quad (2,5)(2,6),\quad (2,7)(2,8).
  \]
- For each column \(c=1,\dots,9\), place vertical dominoes on  
  \[
  (3,c)(4,c)\quad\text{and}\quad (5,c)(6,c).
  \]
- In row 7, place horizontal dominoes on  
  \[
  (7,1)(7,2),\quad (7,3)(7,4),\quad (7,5)(7,6),\quad (7,7)(7,8).
  \]

The removed squares are \((1,1)\), \((7,9)\), and \((1,8)\). All other squares are covered exactly once.

Regarding permission versus requirement: the original board after removing the two corners has \(7\cdot 9-2=61\) squares, which is odd, so it cannot be tiled without removing an extra square. Thus even if removing the extra square is merely permitted, any successful tiling must in fact use that permission. If removing exactly one extra square is required, the same construction works. So in this problem the distinction does not change the answer: yes, such a tiling exists.
